messages.author: b290b67abd35ca2f
messages.subject: CFI and RMSEA not informative?
parts:
Hello all,

If you perform a confirmatory factor analysis using the lavaan cfa() function, how do you interpret values of RMSEA = 0, CFI = 1 and TLI > 1? I've found that if chi square is less than the degrees of freedom, that can cause this issue. That is the case for me here. How would you proceed in this instance? Is there another way of specifying the model? There is some cross-loading in the factor structure, which makes me wonder if this is really a demonstration of high model fit. Here is the code and output:

HS.model3 <- ' f1  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              f2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              f3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9'

messages.author: cf6f800b12f87d14
messages.subject: Re: CFI and RMSEA not informative?
parts:
Hello Raj,

because the chi-square statistic is sensible to sample size and the confidence interval of the RMSEA in your model could still be a bit thinner, I guess recruiting some more participants would be a solution (if this is possible). You can see, for example, Kelly & Lai (2018) for sample size planning for CFA models.

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781118489772.ch5

Best regards,
Hsin-Rui Lin

messages.subject: Re: CFI and RMSEA not informative?
parts:
Raj,

It is related to chi-squared being lower than its expected value (df),
but it is not an "issue." Your model fits well in that it reproduces
the original covariance matrix. It still wouldn't hurt to look at
residuals to be sure local misfit isn't being masked, but there is no
problem at all with this.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: CFI and RMSEA not informative?
parts:
Thanks to you both for your quick responses! They're very helpful.

You both note the chi-square value, but I also saw on another thread in the group that because the chi-square value is not significant as in this case, this can cause the high CFI and RMSEA values. Is the lack of significance a concern? 

On the sample size, I want to note that the sample size used here was similar to one used for a separate study not shown here and results did not yield this kind of model fit. I saw that Bentler and Chou (1987) recommend a ratio of sample size to free parameters of 5 to 1, whilst Tanaka (1987) recommended 20 to 1 (though this seems quite high). In this case, our ratio is around 14.2, which seems fairly reasonable. Would a sample size yielding a ratio closer to 20 to 1 be recommended here?

In terms of presenting these results, say if you were writing them up for a publication, how would you frame them? Would you say that the CFA indicates perfect model fit? Are the values of RMSEA and CFI actually informative here?

Pat, on the residuals, how do I look at them and what should I be looking out for?

Hi Raj,

as I have learned from the methodological literature, the rule of thumb ratio (5:1 or 10:1 or 20:1) is not recommended anymore, one should better perform a power analysis (if possible) to estimate the sample size required given some models which are to be tested.

Best regards,
Hsin-Rui Lin

messages.subject: Re: CFI and RMSEA not informative?
parts:
Thanks again to you both. 

On the lack of significance, I did not realise that this was the goal. I have another similar model based on a different set of observed variables where CFI = 0.95, TLI = 0.936 and RMSEA = 0.063. For this other model, the chi-square value is significant. Does this mean the results are inconsistent with the data? Is the lack of significance also the goal for the "P-value RMSEA <= 0.05" output?

On the sample size, thanks for the suggestion of a power analysis. I looked at the semPower package to do the following a priori analysis:

semPower.aPriori(effect = .06, effect.measure = 'RMSEA', alpha = .05, power = .80, df = 24) 

Which gives the required number of observations as 262 for RMSEA = 0.6 at 80% power (and 325 for 90% power). For RMSEA = 0.05, the required number goes up to 375 for 80% power. I'll have a think about this, given our sample size of 298 is not far off.

> You both note the chi-square value, but I also saw on another thread in the group that because the chi-square value is not significant as in this case, this can cause the high CFI and RMSEA values. Is the lack of significance a concern?
>
> On the sample size, I want to note that the sample size used here was similar to one used for a separate study not shown here and results did not yield this kind of model fit. I saw that Bentler and Chou (1987) recommend a ratio of sample size to free parameters of 5 to 1, whilst Tanaka (1987) recommended 20 to 1 (though this seems quite high). In this case, our ratio is around 14.2, which seems fairly reasonable. Would a sample size yielding a ratio closer to 20 to 1 be recommended here?
>
> In terms of presenting these results, say if you were writing them up for a publication, how would you frame them? Would you say that the CFA indicates perfect model fit? Are the values of RMSEA and CFI actually informative here?
>
> Pat, on the residuals, how do I look at them and what should I be looking out for?
>

>> residuals to be sure local misfit isn't being masked, but there is no
>> problem at all with this.
>>
>> Pat

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: CFI and RMSEA not informative?
parts:
This is getting out of scope re lavaan--the assessment of fit is an
SEM fundamental, and there are many opinions. I'd start with an intro
SEM text. There are some free on the web--Rex Kline's is often
recommended.

Good luck!

>
> On the sample size, thanks for the suggestion of a power analysis. I looked at the semPower package to do the following a priori analysis:
>
> semPower.aPriori(effect = .06, effect.measure = 'RMSEA', alpha = .05, power = .80, df = 24)
>
> Which gives the required number of observations as 262 for RMSEA = 0.6 at 80% power (and 325 for 90% power). For RMSEA = 0.05, the required number goes up to 375 for 80% power. I'll have a think about this, given our sample size of 298 is not far off.
